EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Strong downslope winds developed along the Front Range.  Peak wind reports included:  91 mph (89 kts) atop Blue Mountain, 80 mph (70 kts) at Pinewood Lake and Carter Lake, 75 mph (65 kts) in Boulder, 72 mph (63 kts) at Buckhorn Mountain and 64 mph (57 kts), 2 miles southwest of Loveland.  Damaging winds downed power lines over parts of Larimer and Boulder Counties.  At least 7000 residents in Boulder County alone lost power due to the strong winds.  The wind also caused two fires in Larimer County to quickly spread.  The larger fire near Masonville was human caused and threatened a dozen homes, forcing the evacuation of 65 homes.  The source of the smaller fire had not been determined.  A delivery truck was flipped onto a small van at the intersection of State Highways 72 and 93.  No one was injured in the accident.  In addition, blowing rocks shattered several car windows at an RTD Park and Ride at the same location.

Snowfall rates with this band exceeded two inches per hour.  Accumulations of up to 14 inches were reported in Geauga County by daybreak on the 18th with 8 to 12 inches of accumulation in southern Ashtabula and northern Trumbull Counties.   This activity diminished somewhat during the afternoon of the 18th, but not before another 4 to 8 inches of snow fell from Cuyahoga County eastward through the snowbelt.  Scattered lake effect snow showers then persisted through the 20th.  Thunder and lightning were observed in Cuyahoga County on the 19th.  Total snowfall accumulations from the 17th through the 20th ranged from 12 to 15 inches in eastern Cuyahoga County to over two feet in portions of Geauga and Ashtabula Counties.  A maximum of 26.1 inches was measured in northeastern Geauga County (Hambden Township).  Hundreds of accidents and significant travel delays resulted from this prolonged event.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mammoth 3-day winter storm blasted portions of Utah, just in time for Christmas travelers. The worst hit area was from the Tooele Valley east through Salt Lake and Davis Counties, and east into the Wasatch Mountains. Freeways and side streets alike were snow packed and slick, resulting in nearly 1500 accidents statewide. Amazingly, no fatalities were reported from the accidents and injuries were minor. The heavy wet snow knocked out power to at least 70,000 people, mainly in Salt Lake and Davis Counties, as tree limbs fell on power lines. Almost 10,000 people went without pour for 48 hours or more, causing emergency shelters to be opened in Salt Lake City and Ogden. The threat of avalanches closed Little Cottonwood Canyon and placed Snowbird and Alta on inter-lodge restrictions. An empty light rail train derailed near the University of Utah, with dozens of airline flights being delayed or cancelled at the Salt Lake City International Airport, though one runway was kept open throughout the storm. The 10.6 inches of snow that fell at the Salt Lake Airport on the 26th smashed the record snowfall for the date of 4.3 inches set in 1936, and was the second snowiest December day on record. Some of the impressive snow totals included, Snowbird 65 inches, Alta 64 inches, Farmington Canyon 63 inches, Spruces 53 inches, Solitude 47 inches, Snowbasin 45 inches, The Canyons 40 inches and Brian Head 30 inches. And in the lower elevations, Upper Millcreek had an amazing 40 inches, East Layton 32 inches, Bountiful 30 inches, Centerville 28 inches, Kimball Junction 26 inches, South Ogden 24 inches, Tooele 23 inches, Salt Lake City Airport 19 inches, Spanish Fork 15 inches, Logan 14 inches, Brigham City 13 inches and Alpine, Fillmore and Morgan with 10 inches. It was a skiers dream, but a travelers nightmare.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mammoth 3-day winter storm blasted portions of Utah, just in time for Christmas travelers. The worst hit area was from the Tooele Valley east through Salt Lake and Davis Counties, and east into the Wasatch Mountains. Freeways and side streets alike were snow packed and slick, resulting in nearly 1500 accidents statewide. Amazingly, no fatalities were reported from the accidents and injuries were minor. The heavy wet snow knocked out power to at least 70,000 people, mainly in Salt Lake and Davis Counties, as tree limbs fell on power lines. Almost 10,000 people went without pour for 48 hours or more, causing emergency shelters to be opened in Salt Lake City and Ogden. The threat of avalanches closed Little Cottonwood Canyon and placed Snowbird and Alta on inter-lodge restrictions. An empty light rail train derailed near the University of Utah, with dozens of airline flights being delayed or cancelled at the Salt Lake City International Airport, though one runway was kept open throughout the storm. The 10.6 inches of snow that fell at the Salt Lake Airport on the 26th smashed the record snowfall for the date of 4.3 inches set in 1936, and was the second snowiest December day on record. Some of the impressive snow totals included, Snowbird 65 inches, Alta 64 inches, Farmington Canyon 63 inches, Spruces 53 inches, Solitude 47 inches, Snowbasin 45 inches, The Canyons 40 inches and Brian Head 30 inches. And in the lower elevations, Upper Millcreek had an amazing 40 inches, East Layton 32 inches, Bountiful 30 inches, Centerville 28 inches, Kimball Junction 26 inches, South Ogden 24 inches, Tooele 23 inches, Salt Lake City Airport 19 inches, Spanish Fork 15 inches, Logan 14 inches, Brigham City 13 inches and Alpine, Fillmore and Morgan with 10 inches. It was a skiers dream, but a travelers nightmare.

Damaging winds downed power lines over parts of Larimer and Boulder Counties.  At least 7000 residents in Boulder County alone lost power due to the strong winds.  The wind also caused two fires in Larimer County to quickly spread.  The larger fire near Masonville was human caused and threatened a dozen homes, forcing the evacuation of 65 homes.  The source of the smaller fire had not been determined.  A delivery truck was flipped onto a small van at the intersection of State Highways 72 and 93.  No one was injured in the accident. The combination of an extensive snowpack from an early winter storm and a rainstorm on December 11, produced minor flooding on the Housatonic River in northwestern Connecticut. One to 2 inches of rain fell over a snowpack with a snow equivalent of around 2 inches, melting most of it. The net result was that Stevenson gage crested at 11.1, 0.1 of a foot above flood stage on the 11th. The following day the gage at Still crested at 12.8 feet, 0.6 of a foot above normal. No problems were reported to the National Weather Service as a result of this minor flooding.

On December 18, the second major rainstorm of the month took place after the second major winter storm of the season. Once again, copious rain (ranging from 2 to 4 inches), fell over an extensive snowpack. In northwestern Connecticut it was warm enough for all liquid rain. The excessive runoff once again caused minor flooding on the Housatonic River in Litchfield County. The river crested at 8.1 feet at Gaylordsville, 0.1 of a foot above flood stage. The crest at Stevenson was 11.14 feet, 0.14 above flood stage and the river at Still crested at 12.1 feet, 0.1 above flood stage. No unusual problems were reported to the National Weather Service as a result of this minor flooding.

A strong fall storm system moved across the Upper Midwest during the day. Between 0900 CST and 1500 CST the surface low deepened at about 1 mb per hour.  The strongest winds across Eastern Iowa and Northern Illinois coincided with the surface geostrophic maximum winds and a tropospheric fold that reached down to about 450 Mb.  During the high wind event, about 15,000 people were without power and at least 4 radio stations (WXLP, KBEA, KBOB, and KORB) were known to be off the air.  In Bettendorf, Iowa, part of the wall at Bowe Manufacturing collapsed around 1500 CST.  Fortunately the building was evacuated and police closed down U.S. 67 before the failure occurred.  Many observing sites recorded peak wind gusts in the 52 to 56 mph range (45 to 49 knots) with sustained winds of 30 to 40 mph (26 to 35 knots).  Maximum measured winds were 53 knots (61 mph) by KWQC TV in Davenport, Iowa and 54 knots (62 mph) in Pearl City, Illinois.  At Lock and Dam 11 in Dubuque, Iowa, wind equipment there carried a sustained wind of 49 knots (56 mph) at 1630 CST for about 5 to 10 minutes.  Given the magnitude of the event, known damage appeared to be minimal.  This may be due to the fact that most trees had already shed their leaves for the coming winter.

As a cold high pressure system settled over New England, a series of low pressure systems developed off the Mid Atlantic Coast during Friday, December 5th and Saturday, December 6th.The first low pressure system developed along the North Carolina Coast during Friday morning.  As this low moved northeast, it intensified.  Light snow developed and quickly spread northeast across the area during the morning.  Snowfall became heavy across Northeast New Jersey during the afternoon. Between 4 and 7 pm that evening, a 6 to 10 inch snowfall occurred across this area.  There were major impacts to mass transit operations during the evening's "rush" hours.  As this low moved southeast of Long Island, snowfall intensity decreased and became light across the region.The second low pressure system developed further north and west along the DELMARVA Coast during Saturday morning.  As this low rapidly intensified, it moved slowly northeast.  Light snow became heavy across the entire region by noon.  Near blizzard conditions developed across parts of the area from late morning through the evening hours.  Wind gusts up to 35 mph combined with heavy falling snow created near "white out" conditions that reduced visibility to between 1/4 and 1/2 mile. Rain bands associated with Tropical Storm Jimena, which was passing more than 100 miles south, moved over coastal and upslope sections of the Hamakua, Hilo, Puna, and Kau districts on the Big Island of Hawaii, from near Hopokaa all the way southward to near Ka Lae (South Point).  The heavy rain and showers caused stream and drainage ditch flooding, and ponding of roadways in populated areas over the eastern half of the isle.  The rain and occasional easterly wind gusts of 35 to 40 mph caused isolated power outages as well.  However, no serious injuries or property damage were reported.

An area of low pressure moved east across southern Ohio on December 5th.  Precipitation began during the early mornings hours of the 5th and ended around midnight on the 6th.  The precipitation started as a mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow at most locations.  A quick transition to all snow occurred around daybreak.  By 9 am a band of moderate snow had developed along the U.S. Route 30 corridor from Mansfield to Canton.  The greatest snowfall rates occurred during the late afternoon and early evening hours as wrap around moisture from the low moved into the region.  A total of 6 to 9 inches of snow was reported across the area with the greatest amounts along and just south of U.S. 30.  Most locations also received a light glaze of ice from the freezing rain early in the storm.  Significant traffic delays and numerous accidents resulted from this storm.

Snow and ice fell across most of southwest and south central Kansas.  Snow mixed with sleet or ice pellets occurred southeast of a line from Ashland to Greensburg to Kinsley to Larned.  Strong north winds of 30 to 45 MPH caused plenty of blowing and drifting snow, with every county in the CWA reporting less than a quarter mile visibility for several hours, with occasional white out conditions.  Snowfall amounts were banded, with the two highest reports both being 6 inches, from southern Gray county and central Stanton county.  A 30 to 40 mile wide band of snowfall amounts from 4 to 5 inches fell from just north of Scott City southwest through northern Kearny county to southwest of Johnson City in Stanton County.  Another swath of snow 35 to 45 miles wide, also with snow amounts from 4 to 5 inches, fell from near Meade to Cimarron through Dodge City and Greensburg to near Medicine Lodge.  One more band of 4 to 5 inch amounts fell from extreme northwest Hodgeman County to just northwest of Ness City to near Hays.  Many schools and other planned activities were cancelled due to the weather, especially the low visibilities.  Numerous traffic accidents were reported in Liberal, Dodge City, Pratt, and Medicine Lodge.  Two jack-knifed semi-trailers, on a portion of Kansas Highway 96 between Scott City and Leoti, caused the highway to be closed for an hour and a half.  Zero visibility conditions closed U.S. Highway west of Ulysses for about 3 hours Tuesday afternoon on the 10th.

A major winter storm passed across Eastern Oregon and Southwestern Idaho Sunday and Monday December 28th and 29th. This system brought with it copious amounts of snow to the region. Snow fall amounts ranged from a few inches in the lower valleys to nearly a foot near Sumpter in  Baker County Oregon and  nearly 2 feet near Pine in the central mountains of Idaho. There were numerous reports of 6 to 12 inches of new snow. Strong winds on the 29th caused blowing and drifting snow across the Magic Valley.

An area of low pressure moved east across southern Ohio on December 5th.  Precipitation began during the early mornings hours of the 5th and ended around midnight on the 6th.  The precipitation started as a mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow at most locations.  A quick transition to all snow occurred around daybreak.  By 9 am a band of moderate snow had developed along the U.S. Route 30 corridor from Mansfield to Canton.  The greatest snowfall rates occurred during the late afternoon and early evening hours as wrap around moisture from the low moved into the region.  A total of 6 to 9 inches of snow was reported across the area with the greatest amounts along and just south of U.S. 30.  Most locations also received a light glaze of ice from the freezing rain early in the storm.  Significant traffic delays and numerous accidents resulted from this storm.

The combination of spring astronomical tides associated with the new moon and a weak southeast flow caused by an approaching cold front from the west in conjunction with a high pressure system over the nearby Atlantic Ocean produced minor tidal flooding along the Delaware River. Minor tidal flooding also occurred along the tributaries of the Delaware River. In Camden County, the Cooper River flooded Admiral Wilson Boulevard near Baird Boulevard. Traffic was limited to one lane in each direction and traffic was backed up for up to one mile in each direction during the afternoon of the 24th. At Reedy Island (Delaware), the tide on the Delaware River crested at 7.39 feet above mean lower low water at 1124 a.m. EST. Minor flooding begins at 7.2 feet above mean lower low water. Farther upstream, the Delaware River in Philadelphia crested at 8.47 feet above mean lower low water at 154 p.m. EST. Minor flooding begins at 8.2 feet above mean lower low water. In Burlington City (Burlington County), the Delaware River crested at 9.89 feet above mean lower low water. Minor flooding begins at 9.0 feet above mean lower low water.

The circulation around a low pressure system moving northeast along the Eastern Seaboard and a high pressure system which begrudgingly moved away from New England produced onshore flow during the day on the 14th. This led to minor tidal flooding along tidal sections of the Delaware River and its tributaries during the late afternoon and early evening of the 14th. The high tide in Burlington reached 10.35 feet above mean lower low water. Minor tidal flooding starts at 9.0 feet above mean lower low water. The high tide in Philadelphia reached 9.00 feet above mean lower low water. Minor tidal flooding starts in Philadelphia at 8.2 feet above mean lower low water. The high tide at Reedy Island (Delaware) reached 7.49 feet above mean lower low water. Minor flooding at Reedy Island starts at 7.2 feet above mean lower low water. The low pressure system responsible for the tidal flooding developed in the Gulf of Mexico on the 13th and moved northeast reaching the Alabama coastal waters on the evening of the 13th, the southern North Carolina coast the morning of the 14th, near Norfolk during the early afternoon of the 14th, crossed Delaware Bay during the early evening of the 14th and crossed across coastal New Jersey during the rest of the evening of the 14th.

Intensifying low pressure tracking along the Maine coast to central Nova Scotia produced heavy snow across the region. The snow started during the early morning hours of the 15th. Very heavy snow fell during the 15th with snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times...particularly across northern portions of the region. Strong winds produced near blizzard conditions at times with extensive blowing and drifting snow along with visibilities reduced below a quarter mile at times. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 6 to 12 inches along the Downeast coast...with localized totals to around 18 inches. Across interior Downeast areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 10 to 20 inches...with localized totals to around 24 inches. Across central and northern areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 16 to 24 inches with localized totals to around 30 inches. The 27.3 inch storm total at Caribou ( 27.1 inches of which fell during the 15th ) represented the second greatest snowfall ever recorded.

Intensifying low pressure tracking from the Mid Atlantic Coast...through the Gulf of Maine...to Nova Scotia brought heavy snow and near blizzard conditions to the region. Snow began during the night of the 6th then continued...heavy at times...through the 7th before tapering to snow showers during the early morning hours of the 8th. Winds of 20 to 30 mph combined with the heavy snow to produce near blizzard conditions at times during the height of the storm. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 8 to 14 inches...though localized totals ranging from around 18 inches to less than 8 inches were also reported.

Rapidly intensifying low pressure tracking through the Saint Lawrence River Valley produced strong damaging south to southeast winds across the region. Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph were common...with gusts in excess of 60 mph occurring along the coast with onshore winds. A peak wind gust to 62 mph was reported at Stonington. The winds snapped branches and toppled trees which fell on powerlines contributing to power outages. Several thousand customers lost power at various times. The winds also damaged roofs and signs.

The Maurice River at Norma was above its 4 foot flood stage from 230 a.m. EST on the 13th through 1 a.m. EST on the 14th. It crested at 4.10 feet at 830 a.m. EST at 830 a.m. EST on the 13th.      Storm totals included 2.50 inches in Newport, 2.12 inches in Millville and 2.00 inches at Seabrook. The heavy rain was caused by an intense low pressure system at both the surface and aloft that developed over the Southern Plains on the 9th. The primary low pressure system moved toward the Great Lakes on the morning of the 10th while a secondary low pressure system was forming near the upper air support over the Tennessee Valley. This secondary low pressure system continued to intensify and was located over North Carolina the evening of the 10th, near Philadelphia around 7 a.m. EST on the 11th and in western Connecticut early in the evening on the 11th. This secondary low pressure system helped wring the moisture in the atmosphere from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean onto the region.

A second storm developed quickly on the heels of the first winter storm . This storm affected the region from the evening of the 5th through the morning of the 6th. Gusty northwest winds around an intensifying low pressure system produced wind gusts to around 45 mph during the afternoon of the 29th in Eastern Pennsylvania. In Monroe County, in Brodheadsville, shingles were torn away from one home. Glass was shattered at another home. Pennsylvania State Route 715 was closed because of downed trees and wires. In Carbon County, much of Hauto lost power. In Berks County, about 2,500 homes and businesses lost power, with the greatest concentration in and around Hamburg. In Montgomery County in Upper Merion Township, a snapped pole caused power outages that affected nearby businesses. Peak wind gusts included 46 mph at the Philadelphia International Airport, 45 mph in Doylestown (Bucks County), 44 mph in Reading (Berks County), 43 mph in Mount Pocono (Monroe County), 41 mph at the Lehigh Valley International Airport and 40 mph in Pottstown (Montgomery County). The strong winds were caused by the difference in surface pressure between a powerful (about 975 millibars) low pressure system moving through the Saint Lawrence River Valley and a high pressure system building northeast from the Gulf Coast States.

The third of three major December rainstorms of 2003 took place on Christmas Eve across eastern New York. One to two inches of rain on very saturated ground. The rain melted additional snow causing more excessive runoff and some minor flooding on the Esopus Creek, the Wappingers Creek. as well as the Mettawee and Hoosic Rivers. The flooding lingered into Christmas day. On the Esopus Creek in Ulster County, a crest of 11.97 feet took place at  Mount Tremper, nearly a foot above flood stage. Despite this flooding being a bit more significant than the previous two during this month, no unusual problems were reported to the National Weather Service.

Snow and ice fell across most of southwest and south central Kansas.  Snow mixed with sleet or ice pellets occurred southeast of a line from Ashland to Greensburg to Kinsley to Larned.  Strong north winds of 30 to 45 MPH caused plenty of blowing and drifting snow, with every county in the CWA reporting less than a quarter mile visibility for several hours, with occasional white out conditions.  Snowfall amounts were banded, with the two highest reports both being 6 inches, from southern Gray county and central Stanton county.  A 30 to 40 mile wide band of snowfall amounts from 4 to 5 inches fell from just north of Scott City southwest through northern Kearny county to southwest of Johnson City in Stanton County.  Another swath of snow 35 to 45 miles wide, also with snow amounts from 4 to 5 inches, fell from near Meade to Cimarron through Dodge City and Greensburg to near Medicine Lodge.  One more band of 4 to 5 inch amounts fell from extreme northwest Hodgeman County to just northwest of Ness City to near Hays.  Many schools and other planned activities were cancelled due to the weather, especially the low visibilities.  Numerous traffic accidents were reported in Liberal, Dodge City, Pratt, and Medicine Lodge.  Two jack-knifed semi-trailers, on a portion of Kansas Highway 96 between Scott City and Leoti, caused the highway to be closed for an hour and a half.  Zero visibility conditions closed U.S. Highway west of Ulysses for about 3 hours Tuesday afternoon on the 10th.

Moderate to heavy rainfall late on the 18th and on the 19th resulted in flash flooding and small stream flooding. In addition, an isolated severe thunderstorm knocked down large tree limbs in Huddleston.Runoff from heavy rainfall resulted in numerous creeks and streams out of their banks, some of which flooded roads in Grayson, Roanoke, Bath, Alleghany, Tazewell, Wythe, Carroll, and Bland Counties and in and near Sugar Grove. In Bland County, sections of some roads were washed away by the flood waters. In Pembroke, Doe Creek flooded and damaged a barber shop. Near Lexington route 11 was closed because flood waters pushed debris into the road. In Tazewell county, businesses were damaged as creeks overflowed their banks, especially in Bluefield. In Rockbridge County, Kerrs Creek flooded all along it's reach. In the town of Kerrs Creek it reached its highest level since 1985. Some houses had minor damage.  15 people were trapped on Big Springs Rd between Kerrs Creek and Lexington. There was damage to driveways and fences.  South river had significant flash flooding that caused minor damage to homes, and necessitated a water rescue.In Grayson County, Beaver Creek washed out a culvert (72" pipe), and damaged Rt 625.  There was significant flash flooding in the Fairview area along Chestnut Creek. A woman in her vehicle in the Daleheart area was washed into Meadow Creek and had to be rescued.

Numerous traffic accidents were reported in the Garden City area, but none with serious injury.

Strong winds produced near blizzard conditions at times with extensive blowing and drifting snow along with visibilities reduced below a quarter mile at times. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 6 to 12 inches along the Downeast coast...with localized totals to around 18 inches. Across interior Downeast areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 10 to 20 inches...with localized totals to around 24 inches. Across central and northern areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 16 to 24 inches with localized totals to around 30 inches. The 27.3 inch storm total at Caribou ( 27.1 inches of which fell during the 15th ) represented the second greatest snowfall ever recorded.

This secondary low pressure system helped wring the moisture in the atmosphere from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean onto the region.

Six wildfires blackened about 3000 acres of mostly brush land in inaccessible parts of western and central Molokai.  However, one of the blazes did briefly threaten homes in Maunaloa and forced the temporary evacuation of Molokai Ranch campsites.  No other homes or structures were threatened by the fires.  A helicopter, one of three helping to fight the fires, crashed about 1315 on the 26th of June.  The pilot of the aircraft sustained injuries, but they were not life-threatening.  Firefighters from Molokai and Maui battled the fires; along with Molokai Ranch crews that used heavy equipment to make fire breaks.  The causes of the blazes were unknown, though a fire official said they were suspicious in nature.

A brush fire burned about 2500 acres of pasture land and gulches in Kahikinui on the south-facing slopes of Haleakala in East Maui.  State forestry officials said the blaze did not burn into a nearby forest reserve, but they did say that stands of koa and other native plants in the gulches were damaged.  The fire did not threaten homes or other structures.  Maui County firefighters, with help from state and Haleakala National Park specialists, battled the blaze.  Assistance was also provided by Ulupalakua Ranch workers, heavy equipment operators from Goodfellow Brothers, and state highway workers.  To help contain the blaze, county officials also used three helicopters to drop water on the fire.  There were no serious injuries or property damage.  The cause of the blaze was not known.

A strong upper level storm system dove south out of Canada, and moved into Kentucky by early Thursday, December 18th.  Heavy snow fell over portions of eastern Kentucky beginning in the afternoon on Thursday, December 18th.  Snow began accumulating in areas north of the Mountain parkway, along with ridge tops over other areas during the mid-afternoon hours, with many valley locations not switching from rain to snow until 8 or 9 pm the same day.  While many locations accumulated 4 inches of snow or more, only eight counties recorded totals of 4 inches or more within a 12 hour period.  By about 10 am on Friday, December 19th, accumulating snow ended for locations north of Interstate 64 and along the Interstate 75 corridor.  Accumulating snow ended for the rest of eastern Kentucky by around 6 am on Saturday, December 20th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Four inches of snow were reported in Heidelberg, from a co-operative observer, and also about 4 miles northwest of Beattyville.

This secondary low pressure system helped wring the moisture in the atmosphere from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean onto the region.

Sleet and freezing rain began in the early morning of the 5th, and gradually changed to snow, which was heavy during the afternoon and evening of the 5th. Accumulations by 7 AM on the 6th were (in inches): 8 New Cumberland and Thomas; 7 Bruceton and Terra Alta; 6 Bethany, Coopers Rock, Limestone, Silver Hill, and Valley Grove.

Gusty northwest winds around an intensifying low pressure system produced wind gusts to around 45 mph during the afternoon of the 29th in Eastern Pennsylvania. In Monroe County, in Brodheadsville, shingles were torn away from one home. Glass was shattered at another home. Pennsylvania State Route 715 was closed because of downed trees and wires. In Carbon County, much of Hauto lost power. In Berks County, about 2,500 homes and businesses lost power, with the greatest concentration in and around Hamburg. In Montgomery County in Upper Merion Township, a snapped pole caused power outages that affected nearby businesses. Peak wind gusts included 46 mph at the Philadelphia International Airport, 45 mph in Doylestown (Bucks County), 44 mph in Reading (Berks County), 43 mph in Mount Pocono (Monroe County), 41 mph at the Lehigh Valley International Airport and 40 mph in Pottstown (Montgomery County). The strong winds were caused by the difference in surface pressure between a powerful (about 975 millibars) low pressure system moving through the Saint Lawrence River Valley and a high pressure system building northeast from the Gulf Coast States.

An area of low pressure moved east across southern Ohio on December 5th.  Precipitation began during the early mornings hours of the 5th and ended around midnight on the 6th.  The precipitation started as a mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow at most locations.  A quick transition to all snow occurred around daybreak.  By 9 am a band of moderate snow had developed along the U.S. Route 30 corridor from Mansfield to Canton.  The greatest snowfall rates occurred during the late afternoon and early evening hours as wrap around moisture from the low moved into the region.  A total of 6 to 9 inches of snow was reported across the area with the greatest amounts along and just south of U.S. 30.  Most locations also received a light glaze of ice from the freezing rain early in the storm.  Significant traffic delays and numerous accidents resulted from this storm.

A prodigious winter storm affected nearly all of southeastern Idaho beginning Christmas evening and continuing until the morning of the 27th.  Generally 1 to 2 feet of snow were common across the Snake River Plain and southeastern Highlands with the storm.  In Pocatello, it set the one day December record for snowfall with 13 inches on the 26th.  The storm totaled 14.9 inches at the NWS office at the airport.  High winds accompanied the storms with blizzard conditions in Pocatello during the evening and overnight on the 26th.  Other specific snow amounts from the storm were 20 inches on the east benches of Pocatello with 4 feet drifts.  18 inches 8 miles east of Fort Hall, 1 foot in American Falls, 1 foot in the Idaho Falls area, 15 inches in Bone, 9 inches in Grace, 16 inches at Howell Canyon, 16 inches at Wild Horse Divide, 9 inches at Soda Springs, and 15 inches at Driggs.  The Pocatello airport shut down on the 26th and although not receiving heavy snow, blizzard conditions were reported in Burley on the morning of the 26th with whiteout conditions reported on interstate 84.

The combination of a rapidly deepening low pressure system moving through the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system building in from the Plains States produced high winds across New Jersey. The strongest winds occurred during two time periods: in the morning shortly after the low pressure system's cold frontal passage and during the afternoon. The peak wind gusts of the event mainly occurred during the afternoon. Several people were injured by downed trees. A couple of buildings collapsed. Numerous trees, tree limbs, transformers and wires were knocked down and damaged homes and vehicles. Scattered transformer fires occurred. In some instances poles were snapped. Numerous roads were closed including some major roadways. The afternoon and evening commute was difficult because of many closed roads. Emergency personnel had the added problem with road closures because the high winds were blowing away the plastic and wood road barriers.  Shingles, chimney covers, gutters and siding were ripped from houses and fences were damaged by downed limbs and trees.  Vehicles were damaged by fallen trees and/or flying debris. Awnings were torn away, store windows damaged, roadway business signs were knocked down as were overhead traffic signs and traffic signals. Trash and recycling cans were tossed in the middle of roads. Cart shelters tumbled in shopping centers. Some schools had early dismissal because of the lost power and many scholastic games were cancelled. The high winds made it very difficult to fight fires. It also led to blow out tides at times of low tide during the evening of the 13th and 14th along coastal areas and tidal sections of the Delaware River and its tributaries. Sections of many major roads were closed including the Garden State Parkway, U.S. Routes 202, 206 and 46 and New Jersey State Route 12. About 150,000 homes and business lost power in the state: Public Service Electric and Gas reported about 62,200 outages,  Conectiv Energy  reported about 54,000 outages and Jersey Central Power and Light about 23,000 outages and 400 poles down. All power was restored by the 15th. In Sussex County, a student at the Sussex County Community College was trapped in an elevator for 30 minutes after a brush fire occurred near the College and power was lost. About 1,600 county residents lost power with major outages in Newton and near the Stokes State Forest. In Warren County, a 45-year-old man was injured when a tree fell on him near the Econo-Court Motel on U.S. Route 46. The route itself was closed in several locations because of downed trees.  A house in the Vienna section of Independence Township suffered gutter damage after a tree fell on it. In Morris County, two homes were damaged by fallen trees in Pequannock Township. About 20 percent of Boonton Township lost power. Cranes were needed to remove the large trees. In Hunterdon County, a tree fell on a bus in Clinton Township. No injuries occurred. Sections of New Jersey State Routes 12, 31 and U.S. Route 202 were closed. About 8,000 homes and businesses in the county lost power. In Somerset County, several injuries occurred. In Somerville, seven utility poles snapped at 430 p.m. on South Bridge Street and crushed a vehicle. The 56-year-old driver cut his head. Another uninjured driver was temporarily trapped by the downed wires. In Raritan Borough, pieces of a roof tore away and caused leg injuries to an onlooker. In Bernardsville Borough, a 21-year-old man suffered leg and back injuries after the wind knocked him off his ladder. In the Basking Ridge section of Bernards Township, a postal worker was hit in the head by a tree limb. A tree fell through a house in Bernardsville. In Branchburg Township, students were evacuated from the Whiton School after winds downed a transformer and started a fire. Sections of New Jersey State Route 28 and U.S. Routes 202 and 206 were closed because of downed trees and wires. In Monmouth County in a reverse of the blowout tides, wind driven waters from Sandy Hook Bay washed over the access road to the Sandy Hook unit of the Gateway National Recreational Area. A similar effect caused by Barnegat Bay occurred in Ocean County. About 9,000 homes and businesses lost power in Ocean and Monmouth Counties. Elsewhere in Ocean County, the southbound lanes of the Garden State Parkway were backed up because of downed trees. Power outages were concentrated in the Holiday City section of Berkeley Township. In Mercer County, a roof partially tore off a home in Trenton and a tree fell on a Princeton home. In Burlington County, a driver was uninjured in spite of a tree that landed on his vehicle in Medford Township. The hardest hit locations in the county were Cinnaminson and Willingboro Townships. In Camden County, school children were not injured when a tree fell on their bus when leaving Saint Jude's School in Gloucester Township. In Camden, a large building in the process of being converted to housing collapsed in pieces between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m. EST.In Cherry Hill, the wind fanned a blaze at a warehouse. The wind carried embers to the Woodcrest Development. Oversized insulation panels caught fire apparently by a acetylene torch. In Gloucester County, an addition to a home in Woolwich Township collapsed. In Atlantic County, the Atlantic City Police and Fire Communication Center lost power for an hour. Nearly all of Absecon lost power. In Cape May County, a 28 foot empty boxcar overturned on the northbound lanes of the Garden State Parkway in Upper Township. The Cape May Lewes Ferry suspended service for the rest of the day on the 13th. The high wind damaged the roofs of the Sea Isle City Bar and Hotel and the Lollipop Motel in North Wildwood. In Cumberland County, a Shiloh Borough orchard's produce packing warehouse collapsed. The winds caused a concrete wall to topple sending it into a corrugated metal roof. Two duck hunters were rescued after becoming stranded on a mud flat after grounding their skiff near the mouth of the bay in Dividing Creek. About 20,000 homes and businesses lost power in the county including the county administration building, library and state police barracks in Port Norris.  Peak wind gusts included 67 mph in High Point (Sussex County) and Sandy Hook (Monmouth County), 65 mph in Cape May City (Cape May County), 62 mph in Barnegat (Ocean County), 61 mph in Lumberton (Burlington County) and Stone Harbor (Cape May County), 60 mph at the Atlantic City Marina,  55 mph in Belmar (Monmouth County), 54 mph in Hillsborough (Somerset County) and the Atlantic City International Airport, 53 mph in Hamilton (Mercer County), 52 mph in Morristown (Morris County) and Millville (Cumberland County) and 48 mph in Trenton (Mercer County). The high winds were caused by the pressure difference between the low pressure system in the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system in the Central Plains. The low intensified from a 1004 millibar system over Lake Superior the morning of the 12th, to a 982 millibar low near Montreal the morning of the 13th to a 970 millibar low in the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River the morning of the 14th. Some strong wind gusts also occurred on the 14th and hampered power restoration work. Winds diminished for good during the evening of the 14th.

Peak wind gusts included 67 mph in High Point (Sussex County) and Sandy Hook (Monmouth County), 65 mph in Cape May City (Cape May County), 62 mph in Barnegat (Ocean County), 61 mph in Lumberton (Burlington County) and Stone Harbor (Cape May County), 60 mph at the Atlantic City Marina,  55 mph in Belmar (Monmouth County), 54 mph in Hillsborough (Somerset County) and the Atlantic City International Airport, 53 mph in Hamilton (Mercer County), 52 mph in Morristown (Morris County) and Millville (Cumberland County) and 48 mph in Trenton (Mercer County). The high winds were caused by the pressure difference between the low pressure system in the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system in the Central Plains. The low intensified from a 1004 millibar system over Lake Superior the morning of the 12th, to a 982 millibar low near Montreal the morning of the 13th to a 970 millibar low in the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River the morning of the 14th. Some strong wind gusts also occurred on the 14th and hampered power restoration work. Winds diminished for good during the evening of the 14th.

The combination of a rapidly deepening low pressure system moving through the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system building in from the Plains States produced high winds across New Jersey. The strongest winds occurred during two time periods: in the morning shortly after the low pressure system's cold frontal passage and during the afternoon. The peak wind gusts of the event mainly occurred during the afternoon. Several people were injured by downed trees. A couple of buildings collapsed. Numerous trees, tree limbs, transformers and wires were knocked down and damaged homes and vehicles. Scattered transformer fires occurred. In some instances poles were snapped. Numerous roads were closed including some major roadways. The afternoon and evening commute was difficult because of many closed roads. Emergency personnel had the added problem with road closures because the high winds were blowing away the plastic and wood road barriers.  Shingles, chimney covers, gutters and siding were ripped from houses and fences were damaged by downed limbs and trees.  Vehicles were damaged by fallen trees and/or flying debris. Awnings were torn away, store windows damaged, roadway business signs were knocked down as were overhead traffic signs and traffic signals. Trash and recycling cans were tossed in the middle of roads. Cart shelters tumbled in shopping centers. Some schools had early dismissal because of the lost power and many scholastic games were cancelled. The high winds made it very difficult to fight fires. It also led to blow out tides at times of low tide during the evening of the 13th and 14th along coastal areas and tidal sections of the Delaware River and its tributaries. Sections of many major roads were closed including the Garden State Parkway, U.S. Routes 202, 206 and 46 and New Jersey State Route 12. About 150,000 homes and business lost power in the state: Public Service Electric and Gas reported about 62,200 outages,  Conectiv Energy  reported about 54,000 outages and Jersey Central Power and Light about 23,000 outages and 400 poles down. All power was restored by the 15th. Sections of New Jersey State Route 28 and U.S. Routes 202 and 206 were closed because of downed trees and wires. Snow and ice fell across most of southwest and south central Kansas.  Snow mixed with sleet or ice pellets occurred southeast of a line from Ashland to Greensburg to Kinsley to Larned.  Strong north winds of 30 to 45 MPH caused plenty of blowing and drifting snow, with every county in the CWA reporting less than a quarter mile visibility for several hours, with occasional white out conditions.  Snowfall amounts were banded, with the two highest reports both being 6 inches, from southern Gray county and central Stanton county.  A 30 to 40 mile wide band of snowfall amounts from 4 to 5 inches fell from just north of Scott City southwest through northern Kearny county to southwest of Johnson City in Stanton County.  Another swath of snow 35 to 45 miles wide, also with snow amounts from 4 to 5 inches, fell from near Meade to Cimarron through Dodge City and Greensburg to near Medicine Lodge.  One more band of 4 to 5 inch amounts fell from extreme northwest Hodgeman County to just northwest of Ness City to near Hays.  Many schools and other planned activities were cancelled due to the weather, especially the low visibilities.  Numerous traffic accidents were reported in Liberal, Dodge City, Pratt, and Medicine Lodge.  Two jack-knifed semi-trailers, on a portion of Kansas Highway 96 between Scott City and Leoti, caused the highway to be closed for an hour and a half.  Zero visibility conditions closed U.S. Highway west of Ulysses for about 3 hours Tuesday afternoon on the 10th.

Low pressure intensified as it moved from the Gulf Coast up the mid-Atlantic coast to New England and brought a general snow to the entire region. The event lasted 24 to 30 hours from the early morning of  Sunday the 14th through early Monday. Amounts across the Genesee Valley and western Finger Lakes ranged from six to twelve inches while across the eastern Lake Ontario region one to two feet of snow fell. Specific storm total amounts reported were:  21" in Brantingham; 20" in Lowville; 18" in West Monroe and Redfield; 17" in Fulton; 16" in Woodville and Hooker;  15" in Highmarket, Fairhaven and Macedon; 14" in Fort Drum; 13" in Oswego and Spencerport; 12" in Walworth and Greece; 11" in Webster and Fairport; 10" in Penfield and Rochester; 9" in Victor; 8" in Whitesville and Batavia; and 7" in Geneva, Dansville, Wellsville, Warsaw, Leroy and Albion.  The typical rash of automobile accidents occurred as a result of the wintry conditions. Several injuries, some serious, and one fatality (in Ira) were a reported in the accidents. At the Rochester International Airport, a small plane slid off a taxiway and got stuck in the snow.

The combination of a rapidly melting snowpack and 2.50 to 3.50 inches of rain caused flooding along the Piscataquis River at Dover - Foxcroft. The river crested at 11.1 feet...just above the flood stage of 11.0 ft. Several buildings near the river were evacuated...with water reported in the basements of several buildings. Snow that had been plowed into culverts and ditches disrupted the normal drainage of water. This produced standing and running water on several roads. The running water undercut and eroded several roads requiring road closures.

The combination of heavy rain between 3 a.m. and 10 a.m. EST on the 11th and runoff from the melting snow produced widespread poor drainage and some creek flooding in Camden County. The incoming tide during the afternoon slowed the runoff and exacerbated the flooding. Storm totals averaged around 2.0 inches. In Camden, about fifteen families from Westfield Gardens were evacuated by boat when their homes were flooded by five feet of water. In Cherry Hill Township, up to two feet of water accumulated on New Jersey State Route 38 in low lying areas. The Cooper River in Haddonfield was above its 2.8 foot flood stage from 759 a.m. through 715 p.m. EST on the 11th. It crested at 3.42 feet at 230 p.m. EST.     Storm totals included 2.35 inches in Pennsauken. The heavy rain was caused by an intense low pressure system at both the surface and aloft that developed over the Southern Plains on the 9th. The primary low pressure system moved toward the Great Lakes on the morning of the 10th while a secondary low pressure system was forming near the upper air support over the Tennessee Valley. This secondary low pressure system continued to intensify and was located over North Carolina the evening of the 10th, near Philadelphia around 7 a.m. EST on the 11th and in western Connecticut early in the evening on the 11th. This secondary low pressure system helped wring the moisture in the atmosphere from the Gulf of Mexico and the Atlantic Ocean onto the region.

An area of low pressure moved east across southern Ohio on December 5th.  Precipitation began during the early mornings hours of the 5th and ended around midnight on the 6th.  The precipitation started as a mixture of freezing rain, sleet and snow at most locations.  A quick transition to all snow occurred around daybreak.  By 9 am a band of moderate snow had developed along the U.S. Route 30 corridor from Mansfield to Canton.  The greatest snowfall rates occurred during the late afternoon and early evening hours as wrap around moisture from the low moved into the region.  A total of 6 to 9 inches of snow was reported across the area with the greatest amounts along and just south of U.S. 30.  Most locations also received a light glaze of ice from the freezing rain early in the storm.  Significant traffic delays and numerous accidents resulted from this storm.

An area of low pressure moved across the region and produced some heavy rainfall late the 10th and early on the 11th. This rain fell on top of snow covered grounds and led to melting. The combination of the heavy rainfall and the melting snow produced widespread road flooding of over portions of Maryland during the  morning and afternoon hours. Rainfall amounts averaged 2 to 3 inches. Three water rescues were necessary in Frederick County. 40 to 50 cars had to be moved from a parking lot in a low lying area to prevent damage to the vehicles in Laurel. Several rivers and creeks also flooded. Baltimore County authorities closed a number of roads along the Patapsco River due to flooding. The River flooding persisted through the 13th. In Washington County, the Conococheague Creek at Fairview crested nearly 5 feet above flood stage, and the Antietam Creek at Sharpsburg crested 1.5  ft above flood stage at 5:30 am. In Montgomery County, The Potomac River at Little Falls crested almost a foot above flood stage, and The Seneca Creek at Dawsonville rose 2 feet above flood stage before cresting. In Frederick County, the Monocacy River at Frederick rose 6 ft above flood stage at 3 am and fell below flood stage at 2:30 pm, and the Potomac River at Point of Rocks crested 3.5 ft above flood stage on the 12th and fell below flood stage early on the 13th.

A strong upper level storm system dove south out of Canada, and moved into Kentucky by early Thursday, December 18th.  Heavy snow fell over portions of eastern Kentucky beginning in the afternoon on Thursday, December 18th.  Snow began accumulating in areas north of the Mountain parkway, along with ridge tops over other areas during the mid-afternoon hours, with many valley locations not switching from rain to snow until 8 or 9 pm the same day.  While many locations accumulated 4 inches of snow or more, only eight counties recorded totals of 4 inches or more within a 12 hour period.  By about 10 am on Friday, December 19th, accumulating snow ended for locations north of Interstate 64 and along the Interstate 75 corridor.  Accumulating snow ended for the rest of eastern Kentucky by around 6 am on Saturday, December 20th.
EVENT_NARRATIVE: Up to nine inches of snow was reported on some ridge tops in the county.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate to heavy rainfall late on the 18th and on the 19th resulted in flash flooding and small stream flooding. In addition, an isolated severe thunderstorm knocked down large tree limbs in Huddleston.Runoff from heavy rainfall resulted in numerous creeks and streams out of their banks, some of which flooded roads in Grayson, Roanoke, Bath, Alleghany, Tazewell, Wythe, Carroll, and Bland Counties and in and near Sugar Grove. In Bland County, sections of some roads were washed away by the flood waters. In Pembroke, Doe Creek flooded and damaged a barber shop. Near Lexington route 11 was closed because flood waters pushed debris into the road. In Tazewell county, businesses were damaged as creeks overflowed their banks, especially in Bluefield. In Rockbridge County, Kerrs Creek flooded all along it's reach. In the town of Kerrs Creek it reached its highest level since 1985. Some houses had minor damage.  15 people were trapped on Big Springs Rd between Kerrs Creek and Lexington. There was damage to driveways and fences.  South river had significant flash flooding that caused minor damage to homes, and necessitated a water rescue.In Grayson County, Beaver Creek washed out a culvert (72" pipe), and damaged Rt 625.  There was significant flash flooding in the Fairview area along Chestnut Creek. A woman in her vehicle in the Daleheart area was washed into Meadow Creek and had to be rescued.

Another potent winter storm hit much of Utah, with the northern part of the state the hardest hit. Weather was believed to be the main factor in 2 traffic fatalities. Several hundred minor accidents and fender benders occurred up and down the Wasatch Front, with no major injuries reported. Strong south winds ahead of the cold front caused blowing and drifting snow, forcing Hill Air Force Base and Weber State University to close for awhile. The winds and snow also closed Interstate 15 north of Ogden for several hours due to multiple accidents. Farmington Canyon reported a 3-day snowfall of 40 inches, with most Northern Mountain locations in the 20-30 inch range. The Wasatch Front valleys and benches along with the mountain valleys were generally in the 6-12 inch range, but East Layton came in with 19 inches of fresh snow.

An area of low pressure developed over the Gulf Coast region and tracked northeast into the Mid Atlantic region. The storm produced a mixture of snow, sleet and freezing rain. Snowfall totals across Central and Lower Southern Maryland averaged 1 to 3 inches. Some light ice accumulations were also reported.

Intensifying low pressure tracking from the Mid Atlantic Coast...through the Gulf of Maine...to Nova Scotia brought heavy snow and near blizzard conditions to the region. Snow began during the evening of the 6th then continued...heavy at times...through the 7th before tapering to snow showers during the early morning hours of the 8th. Winds of 20 to 30 mph combined with the heavy snow to produce near blizzard conditions at times during the height of the storm. Storm total snow accumulations ranged from 8 to 14 inches.

The combination of runoff from the heavy rain during the first half of the day on the 11th, higher than normal tides from the recent full moon and a southeasterly flow into Delaware Bay and the Delaware River caused tidal flooding along the Delaware River and tidal sections of its tributaries during the afternoon. The incoming afternoon tide also slowed the discharge from the inland rivers and streams, many of which were flooding. The tide on the Delaware River in Burlington (Burlington County, New Jersey) reached 10.37 feet above mean lower low water. Minor tidal flooding begins at 9.0 feet. In Philadelphia, the tide on the Delaware River reached 8.73 feet above mean lower low water. Minor tidal flooding begins at 8.2 feet. The low pressure system passed near Philadelphia during the morning of the 11th and a south to southeast flow preceded the low pressure system.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intensifying low pressure tracking along the Maine coast to central Nova Scotia produced heavy snow across the region. The snow started during the early morning hours of the 15th. Very heavy snow fell during the 15th with snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times...particularly across northern portions of the region. Strong winds produced near blizzard conditions at times with extensive blowing and drifting snow along with visibilities reduced below a quarter mile at times. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 6 to 12 inches along the Downeast coast...with localized totals to around 18 inches. Across interior Downeast areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 10 to 20 inches...with localized totals to around 24 inches. Across central and northern areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 16 to 24 inches with localized totals to around 30 inches. The 27.3 inch storm total at Caribou ( 27.1 inches of which fell during the 15th ) represented the second greatest snowfall ever recorded.

The combination of a rapidly deepening low pressure system moving through the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system building in from the Plains States produced high winds across New Jersey. The strongest winds occurred during two time periods: in the morning shortly after the low pressure system's cold frontal passage and during the afternoon. The peak wind gusts of the event mainly occurred during the afternoon. Several people were injured by downed trees. A couple of buildings collapsed. Numerous trees, tree limbs, transformers and wires were knocked down and damaged homes and vehicles. Scattered transformer fires occurred. In some instances poles were snapped. Numerous roads were closed including some major roadways. The afternoon and evening commute was difficult because of many closed roads. Emergency personnel had the added problem with road closures because the high winds were blowing away the plastic and wood road barriers.  Shingles, chimney covers, gutters and siding were ripped from houses and fences were damaged by downed limbs and trees.  Vehicles were damaged by fallen trees and/or flying debris. Awnings were torn away, store windows damaged, roadway business signs were knocked down as were overhead traffic signs and traffic signals. Trash and recycling cans were tossed in the middle of roads. Cart shelters tumbled in shopping centers. Some schools had early dismissal because of the lost power and many scholastic games were cancelled. The high winds made it very difficult to fight fires. It also led to blow out tides at times of low tide during the evening of the 13th and 14th along coastal areas and tidal sections of the Delaware River and its tributaries. Sections of many major roads were closed including the Garden State Parkway, U.S. Routes 202, 206 and 46 and New Jersey State Route 12. About 150,000 homes and business lost power in the state: Public Service Electric and Gas reported about 62,200 outages,  Conectiv Energy  reported about 54,000 outages and Jersey Central Power and Light about 23,000 outages and 400 poles down. All power was restored by the 15th. In Sussex County, a student at the Sussex County Community College was trapped in an elevator for 30 minutes after a brush fire occurred near the College and power was lost. About 1,600 county residents lost power with major outages in Newton and near the Stokes State Forest. In Warren County, a 45-year-old man was injured when a tree fell on him near the Econo-Court Motel on U.S. Route 46. The route itself was closed in several locations because of downed trees.  A house in the Vienna section of Independence Township suffered gutter damage after a tree fell on it. In Morris County, two homes were damaged by fallen trees in Pequannock Township. About 20 percent of Boonton Township lost power. Cranes were needed to remove the large trees. In Hunterdon County, a tree fell on a bus in Clinton Township. No injuries occurred. Sections of New Jersey State Routes 12, 31 and U.S. Route 202 were closed. About 8,000 homes and businesses in the county lost power. In Somerset County, several injuries occurred. In Somerville, seven utility poles snapped at 430 p.m. on South Bridge Street and crushed a vehicle. The 56-year-old driver cut his head. Another uninjured driver was temporarily trapped by the downed wires. In Raritan Borough, pieces of a roof tore away and caused leg injuries to an onlooker. In Bernardsville Borough, a 21-year-old man suffered leg and back injuries after the wind knocked him off his ladder. In the Basking Ridge section of Bernards Township, a postal worker was hit in the head by a tree limb. A tree fell through a house in Bernardsville. In Branchburg Township, students were evacuated from the Whiton School after winds downed a transformer and started a fire. Sections of New Jersey State Route 28 and U.S. Routes 202 and 206 were closed because of downed trees and wires. In Monmouth County in a reverse of the blowout tides, wind driven waters from Sandy Hook Bay washed over the access road to the Sandy Hook unit of the Gateway National Recreational Area. A similar effect caused by Barnegat Bay occurred in Ocean County. About 9,000 homes and businesses lost power in Ocean and Monmouth Counties. Elsewhere in Ocean County, the southbound lanes of the Garden State Parkway were backed up because of downed trees. Power outages were concentrated in the Holiday City section of Berkeley Township. In Mercer County, a roof partially tore off a home in Trenton and a tree fell on a Princeton home. In Burlington County, a driver was uninjured in spite of a tree that landed on his vehicle in Medford Township. The hardest hit locations in the county were Cinnaminson and Willingboro Townships. In Camden County, school children were not injured when a tree fell on their bus when leaving Saint Jude's School in Gloucester Township. In Camden, a large building in the process of being converted to housing collapsed in pieces between 7 a.m. and 9 a.m. EST.In Cherry Hill, the wind fanned a blaze at a warehouse. The wind carried embers to the Woodcrest Development. Oversized insulation panels caught fire apparently by a acetylene torch. In Gloucester County, an addition to a home in Woolwich Township collapsed. In Atlantic County, the Atlantic City Police and Fire Communication Center lost power for an hour. Nearly all of Absecon lost power. In Cape May County, a 28 foot empty boxcar overturned on the northbound lanes of the Garden State Parkway in Upper Township. The Cape May Lewes Ferry suspended service for the rest of the day on the 13th. The high wind damaged the roofs of the Sea Isle City Bar and Hotel and the Lollipop Motel in North Wildwood. In Cumberland County, a Shiloh Borough orchard's produce packing warehouse collapsed. The winds caused a concrete wall to topple sending it into a corrugated metal roof. Two duck hunters were rescued after becoming stranded on a mud flat after grounding their skiff near the mouth of the bay in Dividing Creek. About 20,000 homes and businesses lost power in the county including the county administration building, library and state police barracks in Port Norris.  Peak wind gusts included 67 mph in High Point (Sussex County) and Sandy Hook (Monmouth County), 65 mph in Cape May City (Cape May County), 62 mph in Barnegat (Ocean County), 61 mph in Lumberton (Burlington County) and Stone Harbor (Cape May County), 60 mph at the Atlantic City Marina,  55 mph in Belmar (Monmouth County), 54 mph in Hillsborough (Somerset County) and the Atlantic City International Airport, 53 mph in Hamilton (Mercer County), 52 mph in Morristown (Morris County) and Millville (Cumberland County) and 48 mph in Trenton (Mercer County). The high winds were caused by the pressure difference between the low pressure system in the Saint Lawrence Valley and a high pressure system in the Central Plains. The low intensified from a 1004 millibar system over Lake Superior the morning of the 12th, to a 982 millibar low near Montreal the morning of the 13th to a 970 millibar low in the mouth of the Saint Lawrence River the morning of the 14th. Some strong wind gusts also occurred on the 14th and hampered power restoration work. Winds diminished for good during the evening of the 14th.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mammoth 3-day winter storm blasted portions of Utah, just in time for Christmas travelers. The worst hit area was from the Tooele Valley east through Salt Lake and Davis Counties, and east into the Wasatch Mountains. Freeways and side streets alike were snow packed and slick, resulting in nearly 1500 accidents statewide. Amazingly, no fatalities were reported from the accidents and injuries were minor. The heavy wet snow knocked out power to at least 70,000 people, mainly in Salt Lake and Davis Counties, as tree limbs fell on power lines. Almost 10,000 people went without pour for 48 hours or more, causing emergency shelters to be opened in Salt Lake City and Ogden. The threat of avalanches closed Little Cottonwood Canyon and placed Snowbird and Alta on inter-lodge restrictions. An empty light rail train derailed near the University of Utah, with dozens of airline flights being delayed or cancelled at the Salt Lake City International Airport, though one runway was kept open throughout the storm. The 10.6 inches of snow that fell at the Salt Lake Airport on the 26th smashed the record snowfall for the date of 4.3 inches set in 1936, and was the second snowiest December day on record. Some of the impressive snow totals included, Snowbird 65 inches, Alta 64 inches, Farmington Canyon 63 inches, Spruces 53 inches, Solitude 47 inches, Snowbasin 45 inches, The Canyons 40 inches and Brian Head 30 inches. And in the lower elevations, Upper Millcreek had an amazing 40 inches, East Layton 32 inches, Bountiful 30 inches, Centerville 28 inches, Kimball Junction 26 inches, South Ogden 24 inches, Tooele 23 inches, Salt Lake City Airport 19 inches, Spanish Fork 15 inches, Logan 14 inches, Brigham City 13 inches and Alpine, Fillmore and Morgan with 10 inches. It was a skiers dream, but a travelers nightmare.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A mammoth 3-day winter storm blasted portions of Utah, just in time for Christmas travelers. The worst hit area was from the Tooele Valley east through Salt Lake and Davis Counties, and east into the Wasatch Mountains. Freeways and side streets alike were snow packed and slick, resulting in nearly 1500 accidents statewide. Amazingly, no fatalities were reported from the accidents and injuries were minor. The heavy wet snow knocked out power to at least 70,000 people, mainly in Salt Lake and Davis Counties, as tree limbs fell on power lines. Almost 10,000 people went without pour for 48 hours or more, causing emergency shelters to be opened in Salt Lake City and Ogden. The threat of avalanches closed Little Cottonwood Canyon and placed Snowbird and Alta on inter-lodge restrictions. An empty light rail train derailed near the University of Utah, with dozens of airline flights being delayed or cancelled at the Salt Lake City International Airport, though one runway was kept open throughout the storm. The 10.6 inches of snow that fell at the Salt Lake Airport on the 26th smashed the record snowfall for the date of 4.3 inches set in 1936, and was the second snowiest December day on record. Some of the impressive snow totals included, Snowbird 65 inches, Alta 64 inches, Farmington Canyon 63 inches, Spruces 53 inches, Solitude 47 inches, Snowbasin 45 inches, The Canyons 40 inches and Brian Head 30 inches. And in the lower elevations, Upper Millcreek had an amazing 40 inches, East Layton 32 inches, Bountiful 30 inches, Centerville 28 inches, Kimball Junction 26 inches, South Ogden 24 inches, Tooele 23 inches, Salt Lake City Airport 19 inches, Spanish Fork 15 inches, Logan 14 inches, Brigham City 13 inches and Alpine, Fillmore and Morgan with 10 inches. It was a skiers dream, but a travelers nightmare.

Heavy snow fell over portions of eastern Kentucky beginning in the afternoon on Thursday, December 18th. By about 10 am on Friday, December 19th, accumulating snow ended for locations north of Interstate 64 and along the Interstate 75 corridor. Several hundred minor accidents and fender benders occurred up and down the Wasatch Front, with no major injuries reported. Strong south winds ahead of the cold front caused blowing and drifting snow, forcing Hill Air Force Base and Weber State University to close for awhile. EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Moderate to heavy rainfall late on the 18th and on the 19th resulted in flash flooding and small stream flooding. In addition, an isolated severe thunderstorm knocked down large tree limbs in Huddleston.Runoff from heavy rainfall resulted in numerous creeks and streams out of their banks, some of which flooded roads in Grayson, Roanoke, Bath, Alleghany, Tazewell, Wythe, Carroll, and Bland Counties and in and near Sugar Grove. In Bland County, sections of some roads were washed away by the flood waters. In Pembroke, Doe Creek flooded and damaged a barber shop. Near Lexington route 11 was closed because flood waters pushed debris into the road. In Tazewell county, businesses were damaged as creeks overflowed their banks, especially in Bluefield. In Rockbridge County, Kerrs Creek flooded all along it's reach. In the town of Kerrs Creek it reached its highest level since 1985. Some houses had minor damage.  15 people were trapped on Big Springs Rd between Kerrs Creek and Lexington. There was damage to driveways and fences.  South river had significant flash flooding that caused minor damage to homes, and necessitated a water rescue.In Grayson County, Beaver Creek washed out a culvert (72" pipe), and damaged Rt 625.  There was significant flash flooding in the Fairview area along Chestnut Creek. A woman in her vehicle in the Daleheart area was washed into Meadow Creek and had to be rescued.

Moderate to heavy rainfall late on the 18th and on the 19th resulted in widespread significant flash flooding and small stream flooding.In Mercer County, there was significant flooding across the county, as many creeks and smaller rivers flooded. Numerous homes and businesses were damaged or destroyed.In Greenbrier County, significant flash flooding occurred along many streams and creeks throughout the county. The flooding damaged or destroyed hundreds of homes.In Monroe County, significant flash flooding occurred along several creeks....resulting in damage to homes and businesses.  Brush Creek flooded and caused evacuations in a trailer park in the Peterstown area.  Indian Creek flooded campgrounds in the Red Sulphur Springs area. In Summers County, significant flash flooding occurred, especiallly in the northern end of the county. Several creeks and streams flooded. Flooding was worst along Laurel Branch in the Sandstone and Ramp areas.  A truck was swept into Lick Creek off of Rt 20 north of the town of Sandstone, necessitating a water rescue. Many homes and businesses sustained damage, mainly in the northern part of the county.There was flooding along Griffiths Creek, where a car was trapped and its occupants had to be rescued.

Rapidly intensifying low pressure tracking through the Saint Lawrence River Valley produced strong damaging south to southeast winds across the region. Wind gusts of 50 to 60 mph were common with gusts in excess of 60 mph occurring along the coast with onshore winds. A peak wind gust to 73 mph was reported at Jonesport. The winds snapped branches and toppled trees which fell on powerlines contributing to power outages. Hundreds of customers lost power at various times. The winds also damaged roofs and signs.

Low pressure intensified as it moved from the Gulf Coast up the mid-Atlantic coast to New England and brought a general snow to the entire region. The event lasted 24 to 30 hours from the early morning of  Sunday the 14th through early Monday. Amounts across the Genesee Valley and western Finger Lakes ranged from six to twelve inches while across the eastern Lake Ontario region one to two feet of snow fell. Specific storm total amounts reported were:  21" in Brantingham; 20" in Lowville; 18" in West Monroe and Redfield; 17" in Fulton; 16" in Woodville and Hooker;  15" in Highmarket, Fairhaven and Macedon; 14" in Fort Drum; 13" in Oswego and Spencerport; 12" in Walworth and Greece; 11" in Webster and Fairport; 10" in Penfield and Rochester; 9" in Victor; 8" in Whitesville and Batavia; and 7" in Geneva, Dansville, Wellsville, Warsaw, Leroy and Albion.  The typical rash of automobile accidents occurred as a result of the wintry conditions. Several injuries, some serious, and one fatality (in Ira) were a reported in the accidents. At the Rochester International Airport, a small plane slid off a taxiway and got stuck in the snow.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: Intensifying low pressure tracking along the Maine coast to central Nova Scotia produced heavy snow across the region. The snow started during the early morning hours of the 15th. Very heavy snow fell during the 15th with snowfall rates of 2 to 3 inches per hour at times...particularly across northern portions of the region. Strong winds produced near blizzard conditions at times with extensive blowing and drifting snow along with visibilities reduced below a quarter mile at times. Storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 6 to 12 inches along the Downeast coast...with localized totals to around 18 inches. Across interior Downeast areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 10 to 20 inches...with localized totals to around 24 inches. Across central and northern areas...storm total snow accumulations generally ranged from 16 to 24 inches with localized totals to around 30 inches. The 27.3 inch storm total at Caribou ( 27.1 inches of which fell during the 15th ) represented the second greatest snowfall ever recorded.

The third of three major December rainstorms of 2003 took place on Christmas Eve across eastern New York. One to two inches of rain on very saturated ground. The rain melted additional snow causing more excessive runoff and some minor flooding on the Esopus Creek, the Wappingers Creek. as well as the Mettawee and Hoosic Rivers. The flooding lingered into Christmas day. On the Esopus Creek in Ulster County, a crest of 11.97 feet took place at  Mount Tremper, nearly a foot above flood stage. The gage at Allaben reported a crest of 7.87 feet, 0.87 above flood stage. The Mettawee at Granville in Washington County reported a crest of 8.91 feet, nearly 2 feet above the flood stage. On the Hoosic in Rensselaer County, the river crested at 12.26 feet, slightly above the 12-foot flood stage. Despite this flooding being a bit more significant than the previous two during this month, no unusual problems were reported to the National Weather Service.

EPISODE_NARRATIVE: A strong low pressure system moved up the eastern United States coast on the 17th to be in New England late that day.  Rain started on the 16th continuing into the 17th before changing completely to snow during the afternoon.  Wet snow only amounted to 2 to 3 inches across the area on the 17th.  Colder air from the west and northwest was pulled in behind the exiting surface low pressure with surface winds between 15 and 25 mph.  Lake effect snow became organized early on the 18th, then ended as flurries the evening of the 18th.  Snowfall amounts were mostly 10 to 15 inches across the northern half of Oneida County.  In Onondaga, Madison, and the southern half of Oneida Counties snowfall amounts were 6 to 12 inches.  The heaviest snow fell during the first half of the 18th.

Snow showers associated with an arctic cold front caused slippery traveling conditions during the morning commute from the Poconos south to Bucks County. In the Poconos, reported accumulations reached as high as 2.5 inches in Tobyhanna (Monroe County). Dozens of accidents occurred. Interstate 80 was closed for hours during the morning of the 2nd in Pocono Township after two tractor trailers collided. Numerous accidents were also reported on Interstate 380. Farther to the south lighter accumulations occurred. But, on roadways the snow melted, the water then froze and black ice formed. In Bucks County, both the Scudder Falls Bridge (Interstate 95) and U.S. Route 202 bridge were closed heading into New Jersey because of accidents on their respective spans. U.S. Route 1 in Bucks County was backed up because of alternate volume and its own icy conditions. A fifteen to twenty minute commute took up to two and a half hours. U.S. Route 13 was closed in Falls Township.

An upper level disturbance moved across Lake Erie and into northwestern Pennsylvania on the evening of December 17th.  This caused the light lake effect snow already falling to quickly intensify.  By late evening a band of moderate to heavy snow stretched from Lake Erie across Northeast Ohio and into Erie and Crawford Counties.  Snowfall rates with this band exceeded two inches per hour.  Accumulations of 6 to 10 inches were reported by daybreak on the 18th.  This activity diminished somewhat during the afternoon of the 18th, but not before another 4 to 8 inches of snow fell across northwestern Pennsylvania.  Scattered lake effect snow showers continued to affect the area on the 19th and 20th.  Total snowfall accumulations from the 17th through the 20th ranged from 12 to nearly 18 inches.  A maximum of 17.8 inches was measured at Corry in southeastern Erie County.  Hundreds of accidents and significant travel delays resulted from this prolonged event.

An area of surface low pressure over the central plains moved northeast into northern Wisconsin, spreading snow across portions of southeast North Dakota.  One band of snow over central North Dakota merged with another band moving north out of northeast South Dakota.  This produced a finger of 6 to 8 inches of snow from eastern Sargent county in North Dakota, through the Fargo-Moorhead area, and into southwest Norman county in Minnesota.  Wind speeds increased after the heaviest snow ended.  The strong wind gusts did lower the visibility to near zero at times.  School and after school activities were cancelled in West Fargo, Fargo, Moorhead, and in Ransom county.  The North Dakota Highway Patrol advised no travel in rural Cass and Richland counties and flights out of Hector Airport were cancelled.
